title: Video Editing After the Timeline
description: Eleven video tools where the timeline stops being the interface: agent edits, script-to-cut pipelines, browser upscaling and camera raw conversion.
content:
# Video Editing After the Timeline

Every video tool for twenty years has been organised around the same object: a horizontal track of clips you scrub with a mouse. The tools in this group either replace that object or work entirely without it.

Both approaches are interesting, and they answer different questions.

## The timeline, kept but driven by words

[[link:/tools/2268|Arsaze]] is the most thoughtful take on keeping the timeline. It is a real NLE that edits while you watch: ask in plain words, or edit the transcript like a document — delete a word and it is cut from the video as a tracked change you can put back. Press Tab to accept the next edit it predicts from the way you just worked, and any turn can be undone. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Codex and Cursor, and clients can leave notes on an exact frame that the AI can act on.

[[link:/tools/2272|Filmcraft]] is the more conventional browser editor with a large generation layer bolted on: import clips, grade colour and clean audio without an account, then spend credits on AI generation, upscaling, background removal, face swap, lip sync and product video across a long list of current models. The model list is genuinely broad and also genuinely overwhelming.

[[link:/tools/2273|ArtCraft]] is the same studio idea extended to 3D: images, video, audio, 3D objects and 3D worlds in one workspace, with character training so a subject stays consistent across generated assets, plus a moodboard and assets library.

## The timeline, replaced by a script

[[link:/tools/2274|Fluxcut]] makes product demo videos from one paragraph, with approval at every step. It writes a brief naming the audience, the pain and the value, lists the shots it needs, drafts a script timed to each shot, voices each line as its own take, composes music to the exact length, and renders with loudness levelled for the platform. Shots you cannot show drop out instead of blocking the video, and later changes show exactly what must be remade.

[[link:/tools/2269|AgentReel]] handles the footage problem. Paste a voiceover script, drop in hundreds of clips, and the agent screens the footage and cuts a captioned short. Missing shots get generated, and stills become four-second clips with a slow zoom.

[[link:/tools/2270|BakeVideos]] starts from a single line and picks the format that fits: real licensed footage for explainers, AI animation for stories, a phone chat for drama. Script, voice, footage, captions and music are all produced, and every scene stays editable afterwards — change a line and only that scene is re-recorded.

[[link:/tools/2275|MarketMee]] attaches the pipeline to a repository. It reads the code you actually changed rather than the commit message, works out what is new for customers in plain English, makes a narrated video in your brand colours plus an on-brand image, and schedules the post to LinkedIn, X, Facebook and Instagram. Autopilot repeats it on every push.

[[link:/tools/2276|Kario]] is the motion graphics version. Paste a website or describe the video, and it uses your logo, colours and screens, cuts the ums and pauses from recordings, and animates a finished video — with every layer still editable afterwards. Single videos are $19.

## Tools that never needed a timeline

[[link:/tools/2271|Vezur AI]] cleans footage you already have: noise and compression artifacts reduced, detail sharpened, upscaling up to 4x at up to 60 fps. Processing runs in the cloud, the original file stays unchanged, and you compare the preview against the source before committing. It is honest that results depend on source quality.

[[link:/tools/2277|geneva]] is a command-line video editor where an edit is a JSON document and titles are HTML and CSS drawn without a browser. One MIT-licensed binary, the planner and compositor in Rust, codecs from FFmpeg. Every command becomes a document you can print, diff and put in CI. It is the only tool here that treats a video edit as source code.

[[link:/tools/2278|Kino Transcode]] solves the first step of any edit: getting footage out of a camera. Blackmagic RAW, RED R3D, ProRes, DNxHR and MXF convert to H.264 MP4 or ProRes MOV in the browser tab with nothing uploaded, and camera raw is developed with the ISO and white balance the clip recorded.

## Which camp to pick

If your work involves judgement about pacing, [[link:/tools/2268|Arsaze]] is the interesting one, because it keeps the timeline and makes it legible in language. If your work is repetition — the same product demo every release, the same explainer every launch — [[link:/tools/2274|Fluxcut]] and [[link:/tools/2275|MarketMee]] remove the work rather than speeding it up.

And if you are a developer, [[link:/tools/2277|geneva]] is the one to read even if you never use it. Making an edit a diffable document is the kind of idea that changes how you think about the medium.

The common thread across all eleven is that none of them are competing on render quality. They are competing on how much of the decision-making they can take off your hands before the first frame is composed.
tldr: Arsaze, AgentReel, BakeVideos, Fluxcut, MarketMee, Kario, Filmcraft, ArtCraft, Vezur AI, geneva and Kino Transcode split into two camps: tools that replace the timeline, and tools that never needed one.
